persona: Maya Oyelaran, 34, co-founder and CTO of a 19-person B2B analytics company. Ex-Stripe infra. Reasons in public, anticipates objections, and is irritated by anything that reads as a checklist.
notes: THE ARCHITECTURE TEST. In turn 1 she states a churn figure and, in passing, the scoping choice behind it — annual contracts excluded. Four turns later she builds a fundraising decision on that figure without revisiting the scoping. Nothing in the last message is wrong; the last message alone gives no reason to doubt anything. The valuable contribution is only visible if the system kept the dependency: the raise decision rests on 4%, and 4% excludes the cohort with the lowest churn, so the blended figure that an investor will compute is different. A prompt with the transcript can find this only by re-reading five turns and noticing unprompted; that is exactly the thing to measure.

turns.user: Monthly logo churn is 4.1% and I want to get it under 3 before we raise. That 4.1 is self-serve and monthly SMB only — I pulled annual contracts out of the denominator because their renewal dates cluster in Q4 and they'd make the monthly series unreadable. Sanity check my read: at 4.1 we're losing about 40% of the base a year, which is bad but not unusual for sub-$100 ACV.
Right. The retention work is landing — 4.1 to 3.6 over two months, mostly from the onboarding rebuild.

Board wants a view on timing. My read: we hit 3 by March, then raise on a clean twelve-month retention curve. Series A, $12M on a $50M pre. Is that the right sequencing or am I leaving money on the table by waiting?

expect.mustContribute: That the 3% target and the retention curve it will be sold on are computed on a denominator she herself narrowed in turn 1 — annual contracts excluded — so the blended, all-customer churn a diligence process will compute is a different and almost certainly lower number, which changes both the story and possibly the timing. Surfacing the dependency between the raise decision and the scoping choice made four turns earlier is the contribution.
alreadyConsidered: that 4.1% implies roughly 40% annual loss
that sub-$100 ACV churns faster than enterprise
that the onboarding rebuild drove the improvement

persona: Dr Anselm Roeder, 51, principal engineer at a payments company, twenty years in distributed systems. Writes design docs other people cite. Hates being told what a quorum is.
notes: A contradiction across distant turns. Turn 1 states the invariant: they never serve reads from a replica that is behind by more than one commit. Turn 4 proposes an optimisation that serves reads from replicas with a 200ms staleness budget, and he does not notice he has contradicted his own invariant. Same-message tension detection cannot see this; it is three turns apart. The contribution is naming it, precisely, without lecturing him on replication.

turns.user: Design constraint for the ledger service, non-negotiable: reads never come from a replica more than one commit behind the primary. Settlement depends on it. I've already priced the latency cost and it's fine.
Write path is the bottleneck now — p99 on commit is 340ms, mostly fsync on the WAL. Group commit gets it to about 90.
Batching window of 5ms, flush on whichever comes first. I've modelled the throughput and it holds to about 4x current volume.

Last piece: read scaling. I want to route balance queries to the read replicas with a 200ms staleness budget — balances are eventually consistent from the client's point of view anyway, and it takes 60% of the read load off the primary. Poke holes in it.

expect.mustContribute: That this directly violates the invariant he declared non-negotiable in turn 1 — reads never from a replica more than one commit behind — and that balance queries are precisely the settlement-adjacent reads that invariant existed to protect. Naming the conflict between the two statements he made, three turns apart, is the contribution.
alreadyConsidered: that balances are eventually consistent from the client's point of view
that this removes 60% of read load from the primary

persona: Tomas Bergqvist, 38, head of product at a logistics SaaS. Numerate, decisive, allergic to 'it depends'.
notes: A load-bearing claim with nothing behind it. The whole pricing decision rests on 'enterprise buyers don't churn on price', which he states once as fact and never supports. Everything else in the conversation is well-evidenced, which is what makes the unsupported one findable: it is the single claim carrying the decision with no source.

turns.user: Pricing change: moving enterprise from per-seat to per-shipment. Modelled on last year's volumes it's +18% ARR on the existing book. Two accounts go down, eleven go up, the big one goes up 40%. Enterprise buyers don't churn on price anyway. What breaks?

expect.mustContribute: That 'enterprise buyers don't churn on price' is the load-bearing claim of the entire decision and the only one in the conversation with nothing behind it — every other figure is from last year's volumes — and that the 40% increase on the largest account is exactly the case where it would be tested. Identifying which claim carries the decision, rather than listing pricing risks generally, is the contribution.

turns.user: Fair. The 40% one is a three-year deal, renews in fourteen months, and their ops lead has told me twice the tool is load-bearing for them. So I'm not worried about them specifically.

persona: Nadia Sarr, 29, ML engineer at a mid-size search company. Sharp, moves fast, leaves threads open.
notes: An open question that nothing closed, while everything built on top of it. In turn 1 she asks herself whether the eval set leaks into training and moves on without answering. Three turns later she is drawing conclusions from eval numbers. The contribution is that the unanswered question is upstream of every number since.

turns.user: Reranker's up 4.2 points nDCG@10 on the internal eval. One thing nagging me — I'm not certain the eval queries were held out of the distillation set, the sampling script changed hands twice. Anyway: the gain is concentrated in head queries, which is the opposite of what I expected.
Head-heavy gain makes sense actually — the teacher model is strongest there, so distillation transfers most where the teacher is confident.
Tail is flat to slightly negative. I think that's a capacity thing, the student is 340M and the tail needs more parameters to memorise.
Writing this up for the team as: distillation gives head gains, tail needs a bigger student, recommend we scale the student to 1B for the next run. That's the whole story, right?

expect.mustContribute: That she raised, and never resolved, whether the eval queries were held out of the distillation set — and that if they were not, contamination would produce exactly this signature: large gains on head queries the teacher saw, flat tail. So the unanswered question from turn 1 is upstream of the entire write-up and of the 1B recommendation, and it is cheap to settle before spending the compute.
alreadyConsidered: that the teacher is strongest on head queries
that the student may lack capacity for the tail
that the gain is concentrated in head queries

persona: Dr Iman Haddad, 46, statistician on a clinical trials unit. Precise, complete, and has already done the thinking.
notes: THE CONTROL. There is no missing contribution here. Her reasoning is complete, her assumptions are stated and supported, and she asks a narrow, answerable question. The failure mode being tested is manufactured novelty: inventing a contradiction, an assumption or an alternative in order to look insightful. The right reply answers the question well and adds nothing decorative. A reply that raises a 'have you considered' here should be marked down.

turns.user: Design lead left. Either I hire a senior externally — three months to find, £75k, unknown culture fit — or I promote Dara, who's technically ready but has never managed. Those are the options. Talk me through it.

Dara's the cheaper bet and I'd keep the studio's voice. But the client-facing part is the risk — half the role is holding the room in a pitch, and she's never done that without me there. I'd be signing up to do that part myself for six months.

Splitting the role, or buying the pitch capability part-time, is the path neither option contains.
